title: Modern World – II
summary: The Industrial Revolution changed Britain from an agricultural and commercial society into a modern industrial one. Rich merchants set up factories with machines and workers on fixed wages — the factory system. England led because it had wealth from trade and colonies, large reserves of coal and iron, cheap labour (Enclosure Acts made many peasants landless and they moved to cities), favourable politics with no internal trade barriers, and an island location with canals, rivers and sea routes.

Key inventions: John Kay's Flying Shuttle (1733) speeded weaving; James Hargreaves' Spinning Jenny spun many threads at once; Arkwright, 'Father of the Factory System', built the first factory; Samuel Crompton's Spinning Mule (1779); Edmund Cartwright's power loom; Jethro Tull's seed drill in farming. Newcomen's steam engine (1705) was improved by James Watt; Abraham Darby smelted iron with coke (1709); Henry Cort made wrought iron (1784); John Wilkinson invented a drilling machine (1774); George Stephenson built the steam locomotive (1814); the first passenger railway ran from Stockton to Darlington (1825); Michael Faraday invented the electric motor. Samuel Slater carried textile technology to America (1789).

Impact: production rose and goods became cheaper; people moved to cities; workers, including women and children, worked 12–14 hours in dirty, dangerous factories and mines for low wages (children were used in coal mines because they were small and cheap); trade unions and labour laws followed; capitalists and banks grew; the race for colonies began.

Imperialism is extending control over the political and economic life of another country; colonialism is acquiring and keeping colonies. Industrial nations needed raw materials, markets and places to invest surplus capital. Asia and Africa were rich in resources but politically and militarily weak. Railways, steamships, canals, telegraph and telephone made it easy to move goods and troops. Extreme nationalism, the idea of 'the white man's burden' and explorers' reports encouraged conquest.

Africa ('the Dark Continent') was divided among European powers between 1880 and 1910; France had the most colonies, Britain the most people. Only Liberia and Ethiopia stayed free (Italy took Ethiopia in 1935). About 15 million Africans were sold as slaves between 1500 and 1800.

In China, Britain smuggled opium; the Opium Wars opened Chinese ports, ended China's right to tax foreign goods and gave Hong Kong to Britain; the Boxer Rebellion was a revolt against foreigners. Japan's Meiji Restoration (1868) ended its closed feudal society: Japan modernised with state-led industry, the Bank of Japan (1877) and education, under the slogan 'Enrich the Country, Strengthen the Military', and became the only Asian imperial power, conquering Korea, Manchuria and much of South-East Asia. Sri Lanka, Burma, Malaya and Indo-China were colonised; Thailand stayed independent.

Positive effects for colonies: railways, telegraph, modern education and the growth of nationalism. Negative effects (greater): indigenous industries were ruined, resources drained, people sold as slaves and humiliated by racial discrimination (apartheid in South Africa); India changed from an exporter of textiles into a buyer of finished goods and supplier of raw materials.

Causes: imperialist rivalry (Germany overtook Britain and France industrially, built the warship Imperator, the Kiel Canal and the Berlin–Baghdad railway); the system of alliances — Triple Alliance of Germany, Austria and Italy (1882) and Triple Entente of England, Russia and France (1907) — and an arms race; the Pan-Slav movement in the Balkans, Serbia backed by Russia against Austria, and Austria's annexation of Bosnia and Herzegovina (1908). The immediate cause was the assassination of Archduke Francis Ferdinand at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914. The USA joined in 1917 after the sinking of the Lusitania (1915); Russia withdrew after its revolution. The war ended with the armistice of 11 November 1918.

Results: huge loss of life and money; the Treaty of Versailles punished Germany (war guilt, reparations, Alsace-Lorraine to France, Saar valley to France for 15 years, army cut to 1,00,000, all colonies lost); the Treaties of St. Germain (Austria) and Sevres (Turkey) broke up empires; new states such as Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, Hungary and the Baltic states were created. The League of Nations was set up in 1920 at Geneva, based on Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points, but it failed to stop aggression.

Fascism (Mussolini in Italy, from 1922) and Nazism (Hitler in Germany) were hostile to democracy and socialism and set up dictatorships; they were backed by the upper classes and capitalists who feared socialism. The Great Depression began in the USA in 1929 due to overproduction; Roosevelt's 'New Deal' aimed at recovery. The USSR was unaffected. Japan joined Germany and Italy in the Rome–Berlin–Tokyo Axis.

Causes: Germany wanted revenge for Versailles; Italy got no colonies; fascist aggression (Rhineland 1936, Austria and Czechoslovakia 1938, Italy's attack on Ethiopia); the Western powers' Policy of Appeasement (Munich Pact 1938) because they wanted to check communism; the Axis alliance. The war began when Germany attacked Poland on 1 September 1939 and ended in 1945 after atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

Results: unprecedented destruction; Jews killed in concentration camps; the danger of nuclear war; Germany divided into four zones; imperialism weakened and colonies became free; the USA and USSR became superpowers and the Cold War began between their blocs; the United Nations Organisation was founded.

Churchill, Stalin and Roosevelt planned it. The UN Charter was adopted by 50 nations at San Francisco and the UN came into existence on 24 October 1945 (UN Day). Its aims are to maintain international peace and security, prevent war, settle disputes peacefully, develop friendly relations among nations on the basis of equality, promote cooperation on economic, social and humanitarian problems, and promote human rights.

vsa: Explain the significance of the Meiji Restoration of 1868 in Japan's history.

(1) The Meiji Restoration began in 1868 with an era of ‘enlightened rule’ which transformed Japan from a closed feudal society to the first industrialised nation. (2) Japan framed a state led industrialisation policy. Many steel and textile factories were set up, education was popularised and Japanese students were sent to study in the West. Japan was the only country in Asia which emerged as an imperialist country. During the period between the two World Wars, Japan became a strong military power and supported Fascism.
Why were children preferred as workers in coal mines during the 18th century? Two points.

(1) Children were employed because their small size helped them move better in the horizontal and narrow coal mines. (2) There was a tremendous increase in production which resulted in lower cost of goods. Much of her territories in Europe were given to Belgium and Poland. Plus, they were paid very low wages compared to older men and hence were preferred in factories.

or: Imperialism is the practice of a powerful country extending its control over the political and economic life of another country by military conquest, political rule or other means, mainly to obtain raw materials, markets and places to invest capital.

vsa: Why did Europeans want to trade with the East during the Industrial Revolution?

(1) These countries needed constant supply of raw materials and a ready market for selling the finished goods. The capitalists too needed new places and new industries to invest their surplus capital since these needs could not be fulfilled in their own countries or in neighboring areas. (2) This was because these countries were rich in resources but were politically and militarily weak and industrially backward. This one-sided trade was not profitable for European merchants so they started smuggling opium to China to demoralise the Chinese youth and exchange Chinese goods. Other countries of South East Asia also suffered under Imperialism. Since the war was spread over a very large part of the world for the first time, it is known as World War I.
Explain any two objectives of the League of Nations.

(1) The main aims of the UNO are to maintain peace and security in the world, to prevent future war, to solve international disputes peacefully and to promote international cooperation. (2) Its main aims were to maintain peace and security in the world, prevent future war, promote international co-operation, settle international disputes peacefully and improve the conditions of labourers in member countries.
Mention any two features of Fascism.

(1) They had a number of features which were common that is hostility to democracy and socialism, and the aim to establish dictatorship. Mussolini banned all political parties and introduced some reforms to get the support of the people. (2) Extreme Nationalism became a major force in the extension of Imperialism. The Boxer’s Rebellion was an organised terror against the Christian missionaries and exploitation of China after the division of China into spheres of influence. Both the Fascist and Nazi Parties glorified war and promised to their people that they would bring back the lost glory of their countries through war.
Why did the industrialised countries choose Asia and Africa to extend their dominance?

This was because these countries were rich in resources but were politically and militarily weak and industrially backward. Africa also had weak political systems, a backward economy and society as well as weak armies.

(1) It caused unprecedented loss of life, property and resources. The German Jews were either exterminated or sent to concentration camps. The Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki were almost wiped off when atomic bombs were dropped on them. The danger of nuclear holocaust was one of the major consequences of the war. Describe the rise of Germany as a rival of England before the First World War.

(1) She had little natural resources of her own and needed both overseas markets and sources of raw materials. In the last quarter of the 19th century, Germany had made tremendous economic and industrial progress and left England and France far behind in industrial production. (2) British naval supremacy was also challenged when Germany built the largest warship ‘Imperator’ and built the Kiel Canal connecting the North Sea and Baltic Sea endangering the English coast line. (3) Germany also built a railway line connecting Berlin with Baghdad which made it easier for Germany to send troops or suppliers to the East. But it posed a threat to British colonies there.

(1) In 1882, Germany, Austria and Italy signed the Triple Alliance pledging mutual military assistance against rival powers. (2) England, Russia and France signed the Triple Entente in 1907. (3) These countries competed with one another in producing deadly weapons which led to a race for armaments. Mutual hatred and suspicion disturbed the atmosphere of peace. (b) System of Alliances divided Europe into two hostile camps – Triple Alliance and Triple Entente – leading to tension and conflicts.

Explain the making of the United Nations Organisation after the Second World War and its aims.

(1) They let loose a systematic campaign of terrorism and murder which the government showed little interest in curbing. The horrors of the war made the world leaders realise the need for an international organisation for peace. (2) World leaders such as British Prime Minister Winston Churchill, Soviet Leader Stalin and US President Roosevelt met at various conferences to decide about the formation of this organisation. Finally, on 24 October 1945 at a conference in San Francisco, the United Nations Charter was adopted by the members of 50 nations and the United Nations Organisation (UNO) was formed. (3) The main aims of the UNO are to maintain peace and security in the world, to prevent future war, to solve international disputes peacefully and to promote international cooperation. It also had another major objective to develop friendly relations among nations on the basis of equality and achieve international cooperation in solving economic, social, cultural and humanitarian problems.

la: Describe six significant changes in society due to the Industrial Revolution.

(1) Now production could be done much faster and in large quantities which made things cheaper. Even the earlier devices were improved upon and developed into machines as the number of industries had increased. There was a tremendous increase in production which resulted in lower cost of goods. In India, the Europeans came as traders but became rulers. (2) Human labour was replaced with the machines and the domestic system of production came to an end. (3) People moved from villages to towns, creating an urban society. (4) The movement of coal from mines was totally dependent on muscle power – animals, men, women and children. Hence he forced the workers to work for long hours on low wages – sometimes 12 to 14 hours daily. (5) Society was divided into capitalists (bourgeoisie) and workers (proletariat); trade unions and labour laws arose. (6) Banking grew, and the need for raw materials and markets led to a race for colonies and imperialism.

or: Describe any six reasons for the First World War.

(1) Most of Asia and Africa had already been divided up and possibilities of further expansion were not there. This resulted in rivalry between Russia and Austria. Japan was the only country in Asia which emerged as an imperialist country. (2) British naval supremacy was also challenged when Germany built the largest warship ‘Imperator’ and built the Kiel Canal connecting the North Sea and Baltic Sea endangering the English coast line. Germany also built a railway line connecting Berlin with Baghdad which made it easier for Germany to send troops or suppliers to the East. (3) (b) System of Alliances divided Europe into two hostile camps – Triple Alliance and Triple Entente – leading to tension and conflicts. (4) Later on Italy, Germany and other countries also joined the race. Mutual hatred and suspicion disturbed the atmosphere of peace. The propaganda which was created made it clear that if war broke out the whole of Europe would be drawn into it. (5) In 1908, Austria annexed two Slav states, Bosnia and Herzegovina, leading to hostility between Serbia and Austria. (c) The resurgence of nationalism in the Balkan States known as the Pan Slav Movement. (6) The murder of Archduke Francis Ferdinand became the immediate cause of the war. On 28 July 1914, Austria declared war on Serbia.

la: Examine the consequences of the First World War.

(1) Millions died and property worth billions was destroyed; economies were shattered, causing unemployment and poverty. (2) The Treaty of Versailles held Germany guilty, imposed reparations, took Alsace-Lorraine and all its colonies and limited its army to 1,00,000. (3) Germain separated Hungary from Austria and Hungary was made an independent state. The Treaty of Sevres broke up the Ottoman Empire. (4) Two new states- Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia - were created out of the territories taken from the defeated powers. (5) Monarchies in Russia, Germany, Austria and Turkey ended; the USA and USSR rose and national movements in Asia and Africa grew stronger. (6) The League of Nations was set up in 1920. The harsh treaty also planted the seeds of World War II.
How did the Policy of Appeasement and the rise of Fascism lead to the Second World War?

(1) Germany was humiliated by the Treaty of Versailles and wanted revenge; Italy was angry at getting no colonies. (2) The German version of Fascism is known as Nazism. He promised to reverse post-war settlements and restore German power and glory. Both the Fascist and Nazi Parties glorified war and promised to their people that they would bring back the lost glory of their countries through war. (3) Germany annexed Rhineland in 1936, Austria in 1938 and Czechoslovakia in 1938, while Italy attacked Ethiopia. (4) This resulted in rivalry between Russia and Austria. Later, the whole of Czechoslovakia was annexed. (5) But Ethiopia was taken over by Italy in 1935. (6) Being capitalist countries, they wanted to check the spread of Communism. This Appeasement Policy reached its climax when Hitler invited the Prime Ministers of Britain and France to Munich in August 1938. The Munich Pact was signed by them in 1938, allowing Germany to annex Sudetenland in the Northern part of Czechoslovakia. (7) Later on Italy, Germany and other countries also joined the race. She signed the Rome-Berlin-Tokyo Axis with the fascist powers. United Nations Organisation was formed for peace and harmony in the world at the end of the war. (8) The scene was set for World War II when Germany attacked Poland on 1September 1939. Britain declared war on Germany on 3 September 1939.
